findings.finding: Use the isosceles pairs to explore why a congruent pair can have more than one valid vertex correspondence.
findings.breakdown: Both candidates explore the same symmetry. One combined task lets students explain alternative correspondences and contrast them with the scalene Your Turn pair.
findings.checked: In p4-q1-a, fixing B↔E permits either pairing of the base vertices. In p8-q4b, both QPR and PQR match LMN, and angle PRQ remains 36°. The three distinct side classes in p3-your-turn determine a unique correspondence. Matching vertices and writing congruence statements have already been taught.
findings.assumptions: The distinct side-tick classes in the scalene Your Turn represent distinct side lengths, as intended by the supplied diagram description.

repair.proposal: After p8-q4b, offer this optional task: 'Keep LMN as the first triangle's order. Find two valid orders for the second triangle and explain why both work. Does your choice change angle PRQ? Explain why the scalene triangles in p3-your-turn have only one complete correspondence.' Expected answer: ΔLMN ≡ ΔQPR and ΔLMN ≡ ΔPQR. The isosceles base vertices can swap while N still matches R, so angle PRQ remains 36°. Each scalene vertex joins a different pair of side lengths, fixing its match. The same base-vertex interchange explains the two valid correspondences in p4-q1-a.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the alternative correspondences through symmetry and distinguish them from the unique scalene correspondence.

findings.finding: Generalise the midpoint cut by determining exactly when its two triangles are congruent.
findings.breakdown: This extends the existing SSS task into a necessary-and-sufficient condition and a consequence for the cut.
findings.checked: If AC=BC, the halves are congruent by SSS. Conversely, equality of their perimeters, together with AM=BM and the common CM, gives AC=BC even without assuming a particular correspondence. Under the SSS correspondence, the angles at M are equal and supplementary, hence both 90°.
findings.assumptions: ABC is a nondegenerate triangle. Students know straight angles and supplementary adjacent angles as prior angle knowledge; the course separately includes Angle Relationships.

repair.proposal: After p15-q13, offer: 'M is the midpoint of AB in triangle ABC. Show that triangles ACM and BCM are congruent if and only if AC=BC. When they are congruent, what can you conclude about CM and AB? Give reasons.' Expected answer: If AC=BC, AM=BM and CM is common, so SSS proves congruence. Conversely, congruent triangles have equal perimeters; cancelling AM=BM and the common CM gives AC=BC. The SSS correspondence makes angles AMC and BMC equal. They sum to 180°, so each is 90° and CM is perpendicular to AB.

findings.doneWhen: Students establish both directions and justify the perpendicularity using equal supplementary angles.
